subtopic: MR. BALDWIN-FAILURE TO TABLE LE DAIN COMMISSION INTERIM REPORT

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. BALDWIN-FAILURE TO TABLE LE DAIN COMMISSION INTERIM REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects all members of this House. It is based on the failure of the government to table in the House and make public the interim report of the Le Dain Commission inquiring into the non-medical use of certain drugs. I have given Your Honour the required notice of this question of privilege.
Public inquiries or commissions come under the Inquiries Act and are established "to permit the Governor in Council to conduct inquiries into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada or the conduct of any part of the public business thereof." There is nothing in the Act which authorizes the government to hide or conceal, even for a limited time, any report or reports made. In support of that I refer to the report of the commission on security. In that case the government saw fit to hold back part of the report but justified it on the ground that the national interest must prevail.
The very careful wording of the Act constitutes an irrebuttable presumption that the public interest of the people of Canada is involved. This and the fact that the Canadian taxpayer is footing the bill make it impossible for the government to maintain that any report of this or any commission, either interim or final, is the private property of the leaders of one political party to be suppressed or publication delayed to suit the partisan convenience and interest of such people. To do so is a contempt of the rights of this House.
Tradition, constitutional precedent, and the present practice in this country and in the United Kingdom where this type of inquiry originated all support the view that a report must be tabled in this House when it is received by the government.
Nor should the government or any minister be permitted to play games by pretending that the report has not been officially tendered to the government when in fact the contents have been made known.

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN-FAILURE TO TABLE LE DAIN COMMISSION INTERIM REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. BALDWIN-FAILURE TO TABLE LE DAIN COMMISSION INTERIM REPORT
speechtext:
I draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that it is public knowledge today that the commissioner involved has made some serious charges in this regard. In the United Kingdom the present practice is to fix a time limit and publication must be made in accordance with this.
Finally, in this contemporary age of a great public interest, on an issue of such tremendous importance, and at a time when the right of the public to be fully and immediately informed is accepted as part of our democratic system, the failure of this government to be frank and honest and table the report constitutes a contempt and a breach of the privileges of the members of this House as trustees of the rights of all Canadians. This represents a conflict between the "just society" and the "secret society". I therefore move:
That the question of the failure of the government to immediately table the interim report of the commission of inquiry into the non-medical use of drugs be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to consider and report back to this House whether such failure is a contempt and a breach of privilege and for a declaration as to the duty of government to table reports of commissions of inquiry forthwith after they have been received.
If Your Honour holds there is a prima facie case, I ask that this motion be put.

The hon. member referred to the fact that in another jurisdiction there is a rule which specifies a time limit within which certain reports have to be filed. There is no such rule in our Standing Orders. On the contrary, there is a procedure which is specified in the Standing Orders whereby members of this House can obtain production of documents or pro-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave under Standing Order 43 for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion on a subject of urgent and pressing necessity.
At 6 p.m. yesterday the Minister without Portfolio from Windsor West tabled, pursuant to Standing Order 42(2), a letter from the Minister of Finance to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs wherein the Minister of Finance announced changes in the personal income tax rates during the first five years after the coming into effect of the tax proposals so as to neutralize some of the tax increases incorporated in the white paper proposals. Included in the statement is the following sentence on page two:
But I have said the white paper proposals are going to be changed and the changes will substantially reduce the amount available for prospective tax cuts.
Such an indefinite and confusing statement can only create uncertainty and bewilderment in the minds of the members of both parliamentary committees now hearing public tes-

timony on the government's tax proposals and in the minds of the public making representations. Why discuss proposals and changes which no longer are relevant or which may have been materially altered? A clearcut statement of the changes decided upon is called for immediately along with the reasons for the changes. The responsibility rests with the government.
I therefore move, seconded by my hon. friend from Halifax-East Hants.
That this House request the Minister of Finance to issue a concise statement with reasons for the changes decided upon in the white paper on tax changes, and that the same be communicated immediately to the parliamentary committee studying the said white paper.

Any forecast of things to come is, at best, nothing more than an educated guess, and two of the leading educated guessers are Cen-

In 1961, this proportion was 62 per cent as compared with Britain, in first place, with 77 per cent. It topped the other nine nations with an annual rate almost twice that of the next in line-4.1 per cent as compared with second place United States with 2.7 per cent. Fortunately or unfortunately, depending upon how one views urban development, this pre-eminent rate continues. Canada's strong increase in population growth and rate of urbanization is likely to continue until 1980 at least.
The Economic Council forecasts a population of about 26 million by 1980, a growth since 1965 of 28 per cent. This is the highest growth rate for that 15-year period of seven leading countries including Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Sweden and the United States. The council estimates that of this 1980 population of 26 million, 20 million will reside in urban areas. Perhaps of more significance is the estimate that while all urban areas will grow immensely, those which are already the largest will grow most rapidly and disproportionately. With millions of new urban dwellers being pushed into existing facilities, it is not hard to perceive the outlines of some of the problems which will be created.
I noticed in the Ottawa Journal of April 13, 1970, an article by James Nelson under the heading, "Five Million Families Push Housing Needs". It states in part:
About the middle of this year, the number of families in Canada should reach 5,000,000, twice what it was in 1940 and 1,000,000 more than in 1959.

The unfortunate fact about today's development picture is that almost all single-family dwellings are designed for the taste and the purse of an affluent society. Yet the urgent need is not among the affluent; it is largely among the group which lies between the poverty line as defined by the Canadian Welfare Council, around $3,000 per year, and the poverty line as set out by the Canadian Labour Congress-$10,000 or $11,000. The need is greatest in the twilight zone of our affluent society, among those without economic elbow-room who are prisoners of the city.
I should like to put on record what the Canadian Welfare Council said in its statement of April 26, 1970. It read from the first page as follows:
The committee views the current housing situation as continuing to be an emergency for people of low-income and a serious problem for middle-income Canadians. In terms of rent levels, vacancy rates, and mortgage interest rates, it is obvious that conditions have deteriorated since the conference was held in 1968.
It is against this challenge to produce less expensive, relevant housing that the government's taxation policies in general and the white paper proposals in particular must be measured. Against this background, Mr. Speaker, you will be keenly aware of one of the fundamental shortcomings of the government white paper: it covers only part of the tax field. No one has any idea of government policy on consumption and sales taxes. In considering the impact of new tax programs on the housing industry it is surely of prime importance for us to know whether the government is now willing to contemplate any relief from the onerous 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. This demand has been made so often that we proponents of it must be sounding somewhat like a broken record. But it still remains a valid demand.
There are a number of proposals in the white paper which will generate great frustration and confusion for home owners and for people in the real estate business. The major one is, of course, the proposal to apply capital gains tax to owner-occupied homes. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), as I understand it, wants to exclude most Canadian homes from capital gains tax, but unfortunately the white paper does not say just how this is to be achieved, nor does there seem to be any practical and simple method of accomplishing this end. Not only would homes be tied up in endless red tape, but it is noticed there are major discriminatory features attached to this proposal.

For example, a home owner would be exempted from tax if he moved from one area of Canada to another in connection with a change of work. On the other hand, no consideration is given for any other reason for selling a house and buying another- expanding family needs, for example. The value of a home will be fixed on valuation day. How does a home owner ensure that valuation is made in a way which will give him some protection? The Minister of Finance says, "Put your own value on it and we will take your word." But he says nothing about what is likely to happen when a dispute arises with the government over the size of the capital gain.
The minister has indicated that the Department of National Revenue will accept any reasonable value which a home owner may establish, for example, by looking at newspaper advertisements or talking to neighbours. I can see the courts and lawyers having a field day with this idea. Further, will Canadians have the foresight to open new books of account? Will they have proof of every home improvement valued at more than $150 so that costs can be applied against the capital gains they realize when selling? Now we hear that the $1,150 annual exemption on individual homes may not be high enough to exempt most homes from capital gains tax.
This is the kind of frustration which Canadians will face daily if the white paper is implemented as it stands. But having regard to the major housing problems likely to arise in the next ten years, there are much more fundamental objections to certain other proposals in the white paper. Perhaps the most serious is the proposed abolition of the two-level system of taxing companies without the substitution of an alternative. This would strike a severe blow at the smaller construction firms which are so important to our housing program. The incentive to plough back investment so as to expand production would be removed as far as the small firms are concerned. The much-needed growth in our productive capacity would be threatened and, in the face of continuing demand, prices could only rise.
I realize that the present lower rate applies even to huge corporations and the two-level system was often open to abuse. But it is unacceptable to me that the system should be abolished without presenting some offsetting provision to help overcome a capital market bias against smaller businesses. Higher taxes on the major elements of the
June 12, 1970

housing market can only add to the cost of housing, and the less generous depreciation provisions for apartment building will, as the Montreal Real Estate Board recently pointed out, drive rents up faster. While taxation policy alone will not solve our housing problems, it is important that we should not increase the obstacles through our tax policies. Yet that is just what the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and the white paper proposals seem to be doing. Little wonder, then, that many are questioning the government's intention to be more effective in making homes available and in encouraging home ownership. At this stage the government should face up to realities and release from the proposals the personal, permanent residences of Canadians.

So there you have it, Mr. Speaker. The government is being blamed because of its anti-inflationary policies which have not only increased unemployment in this country but have made sure that Canadians will not have the required number of housing units. In regard to unemployment, we must bear in mind the number employed in the housing industry today compared with previous times. I have figures that compare 1969 with 1970. They show that in January, 1969, there were
431.000	employed in the construction industry, and that in the same month of 1970 there were only 416,000-a decrease of 15,000, or 3 per cent. In February, 1969, there were 419,000, compared with February, 1970, when there were 391,000-a decrease of 28,000, or 6 per cent. In March, 1969, there were 416,000 in the construction industry, compared with
406.000	a year later-a decrease of 10,000, or 2J per cent. In April, 1969, there were 431,000, compared with 426,000 in April, 1970-a decrease of 2J per cent.
In other words, there are a further 10,000 people without work in the construction industry. Perhaps they are working somewhere else, but the point is that as a result of government policy we have in 1970 an unemployment rate of 21.9 per cent in the construction industry, compared with 18.2 per cent last year. This represents an increase this year of 3.7 per cent. I cannot understand the government's thinking in this regard. We are living in an urban-oriented society and housing will unquestionably play a critical role in urban life. Unless the government realizes this fact and appreciates that some priorities must be set in terms of housing, the present situation, which has reached critical proportions since the last war, will be further aggravated.

We have on several occasions indicated that alternatives should be considered by this government. I was pleased to note that the minister indicated approval of one of these alternatives on returning from his trip to Europe, namely, that there is some acceptability of the concept of building societies. The other day I asked the Minister of Finance whether the government would review its policy in this regard, but the minister adopted a kind of smart aleck attitude and said that anybody could start a building society. What he did not say was that in order for a building society to become a reality, there would have to be some tax incentives.
I hope the minister will take this question to his colleagues again for consideration. As long as interest rates continue to rise to the present level, which is around 10J per cent, more money must be brought into the housing field. I asked the minister about this matter the last time the committee considered his department's estimates, and he said that CMHC could not put more money into housing. I asked him about the billions of dollars in the pension funds, and he said there were some problems with the provinces in this regard. Although that may be true, I should like to know whether the minister is making any moves to acquire some of this money for housing purposes. I think the minister, in all fairness, would agree that one practical solution to the housing problem these days would be the creation of building societies.
Another proposal we have made to the minister is the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, a tax that has a very real effect at this time. I do not know why the minister has not indicated whether this is feasible at the present time. I understand that it would take $600 to $700 off the price of a house, at the very minimum. Another alternative to present government policy is to control land prices and to limit speculation by having, not so much land banks but by acquiring land that is serviced. I see no possibility of our being able to help those in the lower-income bracket, much less people in the middle-income bracket, if the cost of land continues to escalate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic Party completely agree with the substance of the motion brought forward by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), to the effect that there has been a serious decline in housing in the first five months of this year and that the minister should take immediate steps to stop the crisis that has been created and introduce measures to solve the problem. In fact, yesterday I proposed a motion under Standing Order 26 to have a special debate on this very matter. Yesterday I also asked the Minister in charge of housing to set forth in a statement on motions some of his ideas in respect of meeting this critical situation.
The Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras) has reached the same position concerning housing that he reached as Minister without Portfolio in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. He has indicated that he is a man of
June 12. 1970

concern, compassion and knowledge, but having acquired these three attributes he finds he cannot do what is required to be done and what he would like to do to solve the problems. The minister attempted to do something in respect of the Indians and Eskimos across Canada, but as soon as he commenced to do so he was stopped.
Now he is confronted with the same problem in regard to housing. He now has a new role; he is now the apologist for government inaction. He is the greatest builder of paper houses this country has ever known. He has become the smokescreen of the government. When the crisis emerges, he makes suggestions such as the one he made last year, that in the CMHC budget for 1971 he would bring forward $200 million for what is known as experimental building in order to develop some of the innovative ideas the builders might have. In respect of that $200 million we have not seen an indication of any great innovation. When he knew he was on the griddle for his poor performance in respect of housing starts in Canada, he came forward with the urban council idea. I recall that at the federal-provincial conference in 1967, Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson brought forward the same idea. Members of the New Democratic Party agree with this idea and I think most Canadians would agree with it. It received a cool reception, however, and was not acted upon. I think it would take more than two or three years to set up the proper framework for an urban council so that it would have immediate direction and would be in a position to take meaningful action in respect of housing problems.
I find that the minister in charge of housing has become a sophisticate in housing jargon. Ever since he read the book on housing dynamics he has attempted to use all the jargon referred to in that book and seems to be trying to confuse the issues. I recall that in his first speech after being appointed minister in charge of housing he said the simple way to solve the housing problem in Canada is to build houses, more houses and more houses. But now he has changed his tune and has become the apologist for the government.
If the minister were in private industry, on his performance to date he would without doubt be fired because of his incompetence and inaction with regard to housing. Let me review his record since he was appointed to this portfolio. In May of this year, CMHC figures indicated a 50.1 per cent decline in housing starts in urban centres as compared
Request for Housing Statement with a similar period last year. Now the projection has dropped to 169,000 housing starts for 1970. Last year there were 210,000 starts. This was the first time the country had broken the 210,000 housing starts barrier. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the government indicated it wanted to build one million homes over the next five years. The figure has dropped to 169,000 for 1970. This indicates a substantial drop in respect of achieving the target of one million homes over the next five years.
I recall the statement by CMHC back in 1969 in which it was said that a program even as high as 250,000 emits per year would not create a sufficient stock of houses within five years to bring to an end the overcrowding, doubling up of families in housing accommodation and continued use of deficient dwellings. Here we have CMHC referring to
250,000	units, the Economic Council of Canada refers to 200,000 and 210,000 units and the government of Canada refers to one million units over the next five years. Yet the projection for this year is 169,000 units.
I recall the CMHC budget for 1969-70, which the minister set forth. There was to be a substantial increase in the support of low-income and moderate-income housing. The figures I have indicate that only 27,000 units were built last year, which amounts to only
7.9	per cent of all housing starts in Canada. The minister's projection for 1970 is 35,000, although he must know there are 100,000 people on the public housing waiting lists throughout Canada, and that in Toronto alone there are 18,000. His record with regard to starts is most discouraging. In respect of rents across Canada, the consumer price index indicates an increase of 5.5 points for the 1968-69 period, compared with an increase of 3.5 points in 1966-67 and 4.7 in 1967-68. It would be fair to say that the consumer price index for 1969-70 will rise above the 5.5 points increase of 1968-69. The minister has taken no action to request that the provinces impose rent controls, especially in the major cities throughout Canada, as a measure to fight inflation.
The NHA interest rate at the moment is 10.3 per cent. The conventional rate is 11 per cent, and the rate on second mortgages ranges between 15 per cent and 20 per cent. There has been a substantial drop in the prime rate which the banks charge, and yet CMHC has taken no action to bring down the interest rate charged by conventional lenders, or even by itself on its mortgages. People cannot buy
June 12, 1970

Request for Housing Statement homes at these exorbitant interest rates. With interest rates of 10 per cent and 11 per cent, and with mortgages ranging between $20,000 and $25,000, by the time a person has paid off the mortgage he has paid more than double its principal amount. When we think of a 35-year or 40-year mortgage being assumed by people 25 and 30 years of age, we realize that they will be 65 or 70 years of age before they make their final payment.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
With regard to the financing of homes, we have experienced a substantial drop in mortgage financing by major lending institutions, insurance and financial companies. When the minister appeared before the committee he attempted to put the blame on pension funds, but he did not say that he would get tough and require that a percentage of investment portfolio moneys held by these companies be directed toward financing housing. He did not hesitate to change the 25-year mortgages to 5 years to give the financial institutions a decided advantage with regard to interest rates, nor did he hesitate to free mortgage interest rates. But when it comes to telling the banks and other financial institutions that they must direct a certain percentage of their investment portfolio to the financing of housing, he remains silent.
The record also indicates that home ownership for low-income Canadians appears to have been reduced in the last few years. The percentage of NHA mortgage borrowers in the lower-third income group dropped from
17.9	per cent in 1965 to 6.4 per cent in 1969. With regard to housing, apartments have composed the highest number of building units to date; 52.7 per cent of all starts in 1969 were apartments, compared with 38.3 per cent in 1966. In Toronto alone, of the housing starts 77.8 per cent were apartment dwellings, and in Montreal the figure was 80.7 per cent. This trend to high-density units corresponds neither to the preferences nor to the needs of most Canadians. All these factors have resulted in an emergency for people in all income categories and a serious problem for middle-income Canadians.
After spending a few minutes setting forth the record of the minister in charge of housing, I find it incumbent upon me to tell the House what we in the NDP would do if we were faced with the same problem. First, we would bring forth legislation dropping all mortgage interest rates to 6 per cent. This would help to curb inflation and would stimu-

late home buying. It would help to decrease rents across the country. We would then bring forth legislation, if necessary, to ensure a steady and sufficient flow of mortgage moneys so that homes may be built across the country; and we would give priority to certain types of homes.

I will be glad to answer any questions when I have finished my remarks. We would make sure that residential homes and apartments had priority over shopping centres, luxury apartments, gas stations and other commercial ventures throughout the country. This would be a step in the right direction toward solving the housing problem.
Second, we would ask the provinces to impose rent controls in major cities or areas where it is shown that high rents are contributing to inflation and making it difficult to obtain shelter at reasonable rents. Third, we would introduce new subsidy programs to assist people to purchase or rent homes. In 1969, people at all income levels spent only $20.9 million on public housing subsidies, and the federal contribution amounted to only $12.6 million. This amounts to about 60 cents per person.
Compare that with subsidies for family and youth allowances, which amounted to $29.12 million; subsidies for post secondary education, 13.59 million; railway subsidies, $5.73 million; dairy subsidies, $6.20 million; defence subsidies, $86.22 million. When you compare those subsidies with the 60 cents per person paid for housing, you realize what a low priority the government gives to assisting people with low incomes to obtain housing. It is without doubt a shameful record.
Our subsidies program would include housing allowances to individuals to help them pay their rent. It would include rent supplements to low-income residents in non-profit and co-operative housing. We would subsidize interest rates to all income families, including condominium and co-operative homes. Fourth, we would curb inflation in the cost of land and we would impose a capital gains tax on land speculation. We would acquire large tracts of land with provincial and municipal co-operation. When these lands were obtained, we would lease them and exercise more positive and direct control with regard to land use. If any appreciation in value was obtained as a result of the development of these lands, this appreciation would go to the

public rather than to a private person or company. We would use a minimum of $100 million of the experimental $200 million fund that the minister set up as a start, to acquire these lands, and no sale of Crown lands would be made to private companies.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) questions with regard to the development of housing in land on the Kingston area waterfront. We were told that at this time a private developer by the name of Teron is interested in developing waterfront property in the Kingston area which should be used for public recreational purposes. I ask the minister to direct his attention toward helping people of Kingston develop these waterfront properties for public housing and for public recreational use.
I ask that he contact the municipal officials in Kingston, give them assistance for urban renewal projects in this area and allocate some of the $200 million of the experimental fund to develop this area. To sell this property, which really belongs to the public, to private interests would be indicative of a preference for individual profit rather than concern for the public of Kingston. I ask the minister to apply his immediate attention to this matter.
Fifth, we would develop a program of rehabilitation, because the home improvement loans program has failed as a result of high interest rates and the limitation on the amount that may be borrowed. We would make grants and low-interest loans to enable people to improve their homes. Sixth, we would have citizen participation in neighbourhood improvement organizations, in housing design and development, and in housing management. If we are to have participatory democracy, we must start at the grass roots. Through citizen participation in these areas, the principle of participatory democracy would be fostered.
Seventh, we would set up a separate ministry of housing and urban affairs, and we would have full consultation with all levels of government to assess housing needs. Thus we could allocate housing moneys to those areas of Canada which need housing most. We would give some direction with regard to the type of housing that should be built. We would also set up a Crown building corporation which would use all the newest ideas with regard to design and building techniques in the development of homes. Here we have a house in Boucherville, on the south shore of Montreal, with three bedrooms. The mortgage interest is 5J per cent, with mortgage payments at $71.45 per month. There are other very good homes advertised. Here is a bungalow built in 1970, for $19,750, which has three bedrooms, playroom, fireplace and garage. These homes are in Montreal, close to the centre of the city. Many of these places are within 15 minutes' driving distance of downtown Montreal. They are residential areas. They are not what can be considered rundown areas. I realize this may be exceptional in Canada and that these conditions are not to be found in other places. The area in which Montreal is most lacking is that of public housing. The examples I have given are of homes which middle-income people could purchase with $4,000 or $3,000 down payments. I do not have the advertisements here from the Saturday papers, because it seems our library does not keep the Saturday papers, but I have seen the Saturday papers advertising $14,000 homes with $500 down payments. Montreal, the largest city in Canada, had only tv/o public housing projects, proportionately away behind Toronto, Vancouver and other major cities. A year and a half ago the Montreal city administration finally realized the city was badly lacking in public housing and now homes are being built for low-income people. These are attractive homes and are being built properly.

Another phenomenon of the housing situation in Montreal is the high vacancy rate in apartments, not only in luxury apartments but in middle-class apartments. As has been pointed out by other hon. members, families, especially those with young children, do not prefer to live in apartments. Many of the apartment units in Montreal have fairly low rents, and there are many vacancies. They are in areas of Montreal which are not away out in the suburbs but which still are residential areas.
I understand that the minister will point out again that there has been an increase in investment in public housing, although there has been an increase in investment in public housing, although there has been a decline in housing starts. We who are interested in the problems of the cities were greatly encouraged by the minister's recent announcement concerning the possibility of the establishment of an urban council. No matter how much the federal government may have wanted to deal directly with the municipalities, it could not ignore the views and attitude of an important and significant province of Canada, such as Quebec. That is why it was very difficult to deal with certain municipalities directly, and I can appreciate the difficulty. Montreal withdrew from the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities four years ago, precisely because of pressure brought to bear by the government of Quebec. The announcement by the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras) and the Quebec minister of municipal affairs has greatly pleased me. Clearly, there has been a great change of

policy in Quebec. Not only have there been statements in Quebec saying that there would be co-operation with respect to cities, but last week agreements were signed to establish the first national park in that province. The agreement signed with respect to regional economic expansion will do much for the city of Quebec and the region of Trois-Rivieres. My colleague for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) is present in the House and no doubt will say something in this debate. Speaking as a citizen of Montreal, I would now encourage the leaders of that city to rejoin the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. Since it is one of the most dynamic cities in Canada, it could contribute much to the federation, and it has much to gain. I think the city's counsel would be meaningful for the federation. I hope Montreal will soon take steps to rejoin the federation and participate in the proposed Canadian urban council.
The motion before us refers to the cost of homes and asks the government to take steps to reduce the total cost of individual homes for middle and low-income Canadians. The minister has announced that several research and pilot projects now under way are designed to do that. I have met architects from the Montreal area who are working on programs of this nature and who have participated in low-cost housing programs.
The task force on housing has said, as have many other people, that there is room for great improvement in this area. They mean that the technology of mass production in housing must be improved. Whereas the manufacturers of most consumer products have for a long time reaped the benefits of mass production and new technology, the house builders have lagged far behind. Whereas the price of items inside the home- items such as household appliances and furniture-have been greatly reduced in price over the past 30 or 40 years, the price of homes has not been reduced mainly because methods of mass production have not been used in the housing industry.
I do not think that we at the federal government level can find all the solutions to that problem. It is true that unions involved in house construction have not cleared the way for the implementation of new mass production techniques which could be used. If we are to introduce mass produced housing on a
Request for Housing Statement large scale, we must obtain the co-operation of a number of unions. Also, if we are to build great numbers of mass produced housing units, we must ask for changes in zoning regulations and building codes, and these are matters which fall under provincial and municipal jurisdiction.
We shall also need co-operation to curb land speculation and to build up public land banks for housing purposes. There must be co-operation in the provision of more and better serviced land on which large housing projects can be built. I know that portions of the agreements signed by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) with Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Quebec provide for the establishment of serviced land with sewers and other facilities.

It is not necessary to go over the ground already covered with regard to the housing situation in Canada. It has been clearly established that housing starts were substantially down for the first five months of this year. Housing construction is down approximately 43 per cent. It is down with regard to all parts of the country. The month of May was even worse than previous months. There has been a crisis developing with regard to housing in every province in Canada. In Saskatchewan, housing starts are down 90.4 per cent. In the great province of Ontario, one of the industrial centres of Canada, the figure is down 48 per cent. In the city of Windsor housing starts are down 80 per cent, and in the city of Toronto 53 per cent. The prospects for the next few months are no better, based on information available with regard to applications for new loans.
A few weeks ago, when the situation seemed very serious, the minister estimated there would be 180,000 housing starts in 1970. Is this still the forecast of the minister? If not, how many housing starts does the minister now expect? What is the minister's target? I think the House is entitled to know his expectations. What does the minister propose to do to achieve this target? So far this year the course has been steadily downward. We must speak frankly in situations such as this. The estimate with regard to the number of housing starts can only be the result of horrible forecasting or callous disregard of the implications. I do not want to accuse the minister of callously disregarding the implications because I do not think he is that kind of man. Therefore, I must accuse those responsible for forecasting for the government of a very high degree of incompetence.

I cannot believe that even this government would have sat back had they foreseen what was going to happen and what has happened. This is a very important subject because of the effects on people seeking shelter. It is also important in a number of other respects. It is important with respect to the major fight this government claims it is contending, the fight against inflation. The cost of houses has risen between 55 per cent and 60 per cent since 1965, far exceeding the rise in salaries or wages. The cost of housing is one of the leading components in the consumer price index. It has already been pointed out that this index has gone up and up. In the month of May the consumer price index rose .2 points and the cost of housing rose .7 points.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Moreover, housing is one of the most heavily weighted items in the consumer price index. Clearly, therefore, the cost of housing is a most important factor in inflation. The increase in the cost of housing is reflected in the demands for wage and salary increases; there is no need to elaborate on this point. While we must agree that in Canada, generally speaking, inflation is not due to a shortage of goods or to too many dollars chasing too few goods, the area of housing is plainly one in which shortage of supply is reponsible for the steady rise in cost and, by extension, for the steady increase in the cost of living. In other words, this is an area in which shortage of supply is an inflationary factor and in which a policy of restraint is the worst thing in the world a government could contribute toward reducing inflationary pressures.
Obviously, an important part of any successful anti-inflation fight in Canada is to increase the supply of housing. The supply of housing must be increased, and we must get rid of the tax on building materials. Increased flexibility must be attached to the making of loans for the construction of housing units of all kinds, and this must be done on a regular basis, not on an intermittent basis.
The minister has admitted that the government's policies of restraint have been a substantial factor in the disaster which has taken place this year with regard to housing. He has admitted that the change in taxation policy adopted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in 1969 as far as life insurance companies are concerned has affected their willingness or ability to advance money in the housing market. He has admitted that the
June 12. 1970

tight money policy followed by the government has placed the banks in a position where they have been unable to move strongly into this area. The policy which the government has followed is, therefore, inflationary as far as its effect on housing is concerned, and this is bound to be reflected in the demands of the working man for salary increases.

Now, in the month of June, figures for the first five months of the year are before us and they show some of the results of the government's disastrous housing policy. The Economic Council of Canada had the following to say in its Sixth Annual Review last September. X will read at some length because I believe it sums up the whole question very well.
In view of the large rise in the total housing stock required to 1975 under conditions of rapidly rising levels of new household formation, it is essential that a high rate of new residential construction be maintained, and that there should be no major setback in this sector, such as occurred in 1966. Indeed, over the next year or two, it is particularly important that a very high rate of new housing completions be achieved to increase the relatively low vacancy rates now prevailing in various major Canadian cities. This is one essential requirement for achieving a moderation in the recent very high rates of advance in shelter costs. In these circumstances it is vitally important especially under the financial conditions of today, that the seasonally adjusted annual rate of new housing starts be carefully monitored month by month. If there should be any clear sign that new housing starts are falling off in a significant way, possible remedial actions should be quickly considered. We are now in a situation in which a major housing crisis could develop within a very short period of time.
That is what the Economic Council of Canada said last fall, and I think it is not unfair to say that the government seems to have completely ignored the warning. Yet this is a government which prides itself on efficiency and says that everything is happening as planned. It has bungled, despite warnings from very high places. I do not like to say this, but I think it is true. The only explanation I can find-and I do not think it applies to the minister in question today-is that the government has been so set on getting at labour and picking a fight with it that it has failed to take seriously the developing crisis in housing.
I have been advocating a fair set of guidelines for this country for the past two years. Six per cent is not fair; it cannot be called fair when an increase of 10 per cent occurs in
Request for Housing Statement other places. But the government is insisting on a 6 per cent limitation. We need an incomes policy, but hon. gentlemen opposite have made it very difficult to achieve such a policy in Canada, with public support, because of the way in which they have been behaving.
What is urgently needed as part of any anti-inflation program is a serious attack upon the human misery which has resulted from the disastrous fall-off in housing which we have experienced this year. If imaginative measures were called for in 1969, then certainly bold and imaginative measures are needed today. The matter is urgent because the government has allowed to happen the very thing which the Economic Council warned should be avoided at virtually any cost.
It is high time the minister rose to tell us what his plans are to make more money available for housing at lower cost, whether the government intends to re-examine the level of CMHC loans and make more of them available, and what it will do to end the policy of turning on and off the amount of loan capital available for housing construction-a policy which is disastrous not only for housing starts at any time but in its disruptive effect by weakening the ability of the industry to respond again in a satisfactory way.
I ask him to tell us what the government intends to do about the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and what action it proposes to take to remove the unsettling effects of the white paper proposals as far as they concern home ownership. I call upon the minister to answer these questions. I do not ask him to explain what has happened. I know what has happened: the government has bungled; the government has allowed housing starts to settle to a disastrously low rate. This has happened as a direct result of government policies. The government must accept full responsibility for what has occurred.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
A number of suggestions have been made from the opposition side of the House. More money should be made available for housing, and the cost of the money lowered. Let the government reduce the cost of building materials by eliminating the sales tax. The problem of housing is a long-term one, but I address myself this afternoon particularly to the immediate emergency in which the country finds itself in the field of housing as the
June 12, 1970

Request for Housing Statement direct result of the policies of this government. I ask the minister to get off his seat and to tell the House and the country what he proposes to do about the situation.

Mr. Speaker, from reading the motion, it is easy, I think, to realize that the mover, the hon, member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), is good-natured, mature and broad-minded. He could have said, with some malice not often heard from him, that this House wants to blame the government. But far from doing so, he proposes that, and I quote:
This House declares that the government must, in view of the disastrous decline In residential housing construction, announce before the summer recess new measures to stimulate a signifiant expansion in the number of housing units being built, to reduce the total cost of individual homes for middle and low income Canadians, and to reduce or eliminate unemployment in the construction trades.
At first glance, the motion seems mild. In fact, it refrains from blaming the government too strongly, and I guess that the mover, even if he sits in the opposition, realizes that the

housing shortage is a problem for which not only the government is responsible.
There are several factors. For instance, the scarcity of available capital, the rise in interest rates-for which the government is not necessarily responsible-and the disastrous strikes which occurred in Quebec when certain labour unions refused to co-operate with the government. All these factors played a part in the economic slowdown in the construction field.
When the mover asks the minister to announce measures, I have the impression that he will not have to wait too long and that he might learn a great deal this afternoon because we on the government side know that the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras) is very active and deeply concerned about the housing construction problem in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to relate certain recent decisions to the construction problem.
First of all, I would like to thank the government, and especially the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand), for having designated Trois-Rivieres as a special area. The latter recently announced measures which will improve the substructure of my area and therefore will facilitate not only the establishment of new businesses but also the construction of new houses.
I am particularly grateful to the government for having taken this decision which was welcomed by the population. It had the effect of a shot in the arm for our economy. As everyone knows, activity in the building trade is a sign of general prosperity. That is why we are all in favour of incentives for construction. The minister could give more details than I could and he will be able to do so when he speaks this afternoon. I would also like to comment the recent statements made by the Quebec Minister of Municipal Affairs. He said that he was hoping for better co-operation among the three levels of government.
This is not a new request, but I am pleased to note that for the first time in several years, when we are all wishing for an improved climate among the three levels of government, the Quebec Minister of Municipal Affairs, who is a former mayor and president of the Union of Quebec Municipalities and who is quite aware of the problem, has just made the statement that the Canadian Federation of Mayors has been asking for for several years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 15 minutes it is impossible to cover the subject before us. Many of the details have already been dealt with. I want to start by saying in the presence of the minister that a simple fact is that in the field of housing and urban affairs this government has fiddled and diddled for the last two and more years, with disastrous consequences for Canada and for the people of Canada.
This minister, like the minister before him, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), and like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) so often, has developed a rather disarming habit of sounding cheerful about the situation. The minister always expresses concern for and great sympathy with the disadvantaged people. Indeed, he is always full of concern and pain, but completely empty of policy and action. His concern and sympathy will not build homes. They will not provide accommodation for the disadvantaged people of Canada. However sincere he may be-and I do not doubt his sincerity-the fact is that for years now the housing situation in Canada has gone from bad to worse. The government has stood still without taking any of the steps that might have enabled it to improve the
June 12, 1970	COMMONS
situation, so that every year we are in a worse situation than we were in the year before.
Mr. Speaker, all of us in the opposition-I know I am, and I am sure all my colleagues in the New Democratic Party are-are aware of the fact that the housing problem in a sense is a universal one. There are very few cities in very few countries of the world that have been able to keep up adequately and quickly enough with the rapid urbanization which has been taking place in the last several decades in all the industrialized centres and countries of the world. No one can expect this or any other government to solve the problem overnight, because it is a cumulative problem which results from the rapid urbanization which is more rapid in Canada than anywhere else.
It is a problem which cannot be solved except in the course of some years. Perhaps it cannot be completely solved except in the course of a generation. It is precisely because of this fact that I say to the minister, with all the seriousness of which I am capable, that the fact that there has been an accumulation of decades of mismanagement in the past, together with the fact that this is the result of rapid urbanization which grows year after year, and the fact that it might be years before we can solve the housing problem, is all the more reason this government should be soundly condemned for not having taken the first steps toward a solution.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
No one expects miracles from the minister, but one did expect from the Prime Minister, the swinger of 1968, and from this government some kind of modern approach to this problem, some recognition of the urgency of the problem. We expected some steps which would indicate that we were making at least a modest start on licking the problem of the shortage of housing, of the slums in the cities, of the deteriorating homes in which people have to live, of the overcrowding, of little children playing in the streets because of the absence of parks and playgrounds in our cities, of the traffic jams in the cities, of the air and water pollution and of all those things about which government spokesmen have sounded lyrical and poetical for years now. That is why I for one was forced to say to the conference of mayors and municipalities, at which I had the pleasure of speaking last Tuesday at lunch, that it seems to me these problems are so overwhelming now that they have become almost entirely unmanageable.

The failure of this minister to do the least that should be done with respect to solving these problems, his failure to take some fundamental approaches in this respect, makes the problems worse every day. It is not as if this or the former government were not fully aware of this problem. I re-read only this morning, in preparation for my comments now, a speech which the former Prime Minister, Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, made to a federal-provincial conference on housing and urban development held in Ottawa on December 11, 1967. At that time Mr. Pearson said:
Although every level of government has had its failures in this increasingly vital area of our national and local life, fortunately we still have time in Canada to correct our mistakes and to avoid repeating them in the future.
It is a pity that the present Prime Minister was perhaps absent when Mr. Pearson made the statement, because we still had a little time then. We still have a little time now, but we are not correcting our mistakes and apparently we will not avoid repeating them in the future. On the contrary, we continue to compound them and to make the situation worse. Mr. Pearson in the speech to which I have referred also made the following comment which I draw to the attention of the minister and of the Prime Minister. Having said earlier that there were difficulties and limitations as to jurisdiction, he said:
But the urban environment is now of such fundamental importance to every aspect of Canadian life, including the health of the whole nation and its economy, that local problems in all areas of the country collectively present a national problem which clearly concerns the federal government.
This was said on December 11, 1967, and I am certain that if I looked through Hansard and if I had the time to re-read speeches made by Mr. Pearson and other people in the years before 1967, I would find exactly the same kind of statement-that our program until now has been a failure, that we still have some time to correct our failures, and that all of this is a national concern and a national responsibility. But as I look at the picture in 1970 as compared with 1967, I see that the housing situation now is worse. The price of our houses has gone up, our rents have gone up and the total urban picture has become worse since December 11, 1967. This government, as is apparent from what we see all around us, stands clearly condemned for total failure in the important national area of housing and urban affairs.
It is not as if construction has not been going on. You cannot visit any city in this
June 12, 1970

Request for Housing Statement country without seeing construction taking place, unless there is a construction strike. There is not a city in this country-and I have been to many cities in recent months- where you do not see luxury apartment buildings going up, entirely unnecessary office buildings and unnecessary and redundant commercial buildings going up, whether they be shopping plazas or service stations at some corner, the only corner that is left at the intersection, all the other corners already being occupied by gas stations or bank buildings. It is not as if construction was not going on in Canada, but in social terms it is totally unnecessary construction.
If the funds, the effort, the labour and the resources which are spent in this field of socially unnecessary and less than useful construction at this particular time were turned over to the construction of public housing, to the rehabilitation of old homes, and planning and beautifying the cities, we would not be in the serious difficulties in which we now find ourselves.
I do not make any apology for emphasizing the social philosophy I and my colleagues have often expressed in this House. Our present housing crisis is one of the most visible results of the total failure to organize our society and our economy, of our inclination to leave it to private developers-as I said to the conference of mayors and municipalities in Halifax-to shape our cities, because in the long run they are the ones who do so. They decide what kind of construction they will undertake and they make the decision as to what kind of plan they want, even though municipalities frequently have plans and zoning by-laws. As I said to the conference, I do not know of any single case where the objectives of the municipal plan have not been bent, and perhaps even abandoned as a result of the pressures and the lobbying of the private interests which conflict with the public goals which the municipal councils and planning agencies have set for the city.
We have permitted the private developers to do this. I do not condemn them; they are playing according to the rules as they know them and they are interested in profit, which is why they are in business. They are interested in a situation which will maximize that profit. But I do condemn government at all levels for its failure to demand that our cities be planned, that the people in the cities, rather than the private developers, have something to say about the shape of our

urban environment, and that we set priorities for the use of capital and resources for construction.
Top priority should be given to public housing. The second priority should be given to area development and rehabilitation, and the third priority should be given to low-cost housing for the lower and middle-income people. Only when these priorities in construction are met should we permit the building of banks, office buildings and high-rise luxury apartment houses. These are the priorities that we should set for ourselves in Canada. This is the only way in which this problem can be tackled. It will not be solved in a year or two, but it should be tackled so that the people can have hope that it will be solved, that the quality of our urban life will not be undermined and that the hopelessness of a great many of our low-income people can be removed and some hope given them.
I think my time is about up, so I will draw my remarks to a conclusion. I know that in the files in my office-and I am sure in the files of every hon. member of every party- there are literally hundreds of letters written over the last few years by old people, people with families, young people who cannot afford to pay the rent they are forced to pay, who cannot buy the homes they want to buy, who have nothing left to eat after they have paid the rent, who are on welfare, who are on a long waiting list for public housing and who are totally desperate about their position with regard to accommodation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin m-remarks by saying I appreciate the job which the Minister without Portfolio responsible for housing (Mr. Andras) has done. His approach has been one of genuine concern for the people who make up urban Canada.
All too often we forget that our cities are made up of people, the people who work in them and the people who live in them. There is a tendency to think of our urban areas as consisting of so many houses, apartment buildings, offices, industries and freeways. The minister has avoided this pitfall and has attended admirably to the needs of those who, because their incomes are low, have despaired in the past of ever getting suitable accommodation at reasonable cost. Under the minister's guidance, the housing stock available to low-income families and to our senior citizens has grown significantly and will continue to grow.
However, the fact remains that overall the number of housing starts is down to an unfor-giveable amount. This should really come as no surprise to some of us. It was painfully obvious months ago that this would be a bad year in terms of the number of housing units

begun. The reasons for this are simple, even if the solutions are not: inflation, the tight financial situation and labour disputes. Yet even when it was clear that massive assistance would be required if we were to do our part this year to arrive at the goal of 1.1 million units which the Economic Council has set for the period 1970-1975, the government did not respond. I could understand this if money were not available. But when I see millions of dollars going into the Lift program, when I see the government making available to the provincial governments $300 million more than originally provided for in the current fiscal year, when I see vast amounts being spent on regional development projects, I know that money can be made available if the government deems it desirable.
We have here a question of priorities. The government must surely count housing and urban affairs as being deserving of very high priority. Yet it has not given this impression. Why? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the finger of blame points in a number of directions. First, I have to admit that part of the blame must rest with those, such as myself, in the backbenches of this party who have not spoken out often enough or loudly enough on urban affairs and who have stood idly by while the frontbench has made housing the whipping-boy for inflation. There have been exceptions among the backbenchers, such as the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) and the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney), but by and large the backbenchers of this party have not put the case for the cities strongly enough.
* (3:30 p.m.)
Secondly, I blame the opposition parties. Every goverment needs to be prodded, and this government is no exception. But it seems the opposition contains more plodders than prodders. Certainly some members, such as the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), have presented constructive suggestions to the government and tried to alert their colleagues to the importance of the housing crisis. But clearly these members have not been successful in converting their colleagues, because every day this chamber echoes to the cries of rape-seed and the ghost of the Newfie Bullet.
If the government is to be convinced of the importance of the housing problem, all interested parties must maximize their input
June 12, 1970	COMMONS
into the decision-making process. Where does the National Housebuilders' Association maintain its headquarters? In Toronto! It should be here in Ottawa where officers of the association could be in daily contact with government and its officials and be in a position to influence government policy rather than just react to it. Likewise, I charge the real estate fraternity of this country with not making its problems more apparent to the government. There can be no denying that some of the blame for the housing situation today lies with the real estate people themselves.
The housing crisis cannot be viewed in isolation from the sum of the problems plaguing our cities. It is an integral part of the urban dilemma which can be solved only within a unified framework. We must-I repeat, must-establish a department of urban affairs. For too long we have developed piecemeal programs with little or no understanding of how each would affect the other. We have failed to recognize the basic fact that our urban environment is a complex system constantly interacting with itself.
We have failed to come to grips with the concept of the urban unit and how that total unit will react to new programs and developments. We have, in fact, proceeded as if we were operating in a vacuum. Housing problems have been tackled as if the urban context were irrelevant. This kind of thinking, or perhaps I should say lack of thinking, cannot go on if we value our existence as an urban society. A department of urban affairs would serve to develop and co-ordinate urban policy, and the minister in charge of this department would then be in a position to see that programs affecting our urban areas produce harmony rather than conflict, gardens rather than ghettos.
Surely, if the problems of agriculture require the attention of two full-time ministers and the fiscal operation of this country demands the efforts of two cabinet members, then the problems of urban Canada in which 70 per cent of our people now live and in which 85 per cent will live in the year 2000 are worthy of the attention of a full ministry. And, Mr. Speaker, if I may make a suggestion to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Andras), would be an excellent choice for minister of urban affairs.
I have some further suggestions for government action now. I believe the government should announce for this fall a large mort-
DEBATES	8075
Request for Housing Statement gage commitment for medium and low priced houses and condominium development. This mortgage money should be made available at a rate of no more than 8 per cent. This action would have the effect of lowering competitive interest rates without subsidization and would at the same time reduce unemployment in the construction trades. As hon. members may know, 40 per cent of the cost of a house is on-site labour. The great rush of housing starts which would result from a program such as I am proposing would not only serve to improve the housing stock for middle income Canadians, but would have a very significant and beneficial effect on the unemployment situation.
Further, the government must bring extreme pressure on the banks of Canada to meet the challenge of the housing crisis. But how have these institutions responded to date? They have upped interest rates and they have tightened conditions borrowers must meet. The conventional insurance lenders have gone even further; they are demanding exorbitant equity positions, thus increasing their own profits. This is of no help in meeting the housing crisis. The government must demand that these offenders adjust their policies in order to meet the challenge.
The federal government must also consider offsetting the effects of the white paper on tax reform, which has created a marked decrease in large apartment projects. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to contribute, in a very modest
way, to the debate on the motion proposed today on housing. I think the choice could not have been wiser in view of the sorry and desperate plight of the greater part of our population in this field.
We all agree that the proposals of this government have only brought inadequate results. Some will even say that the government has done nothing, but I will go even further. However, it is to be wondered whether the government has done enough and whether it might not do more. I think we can answer this question.
For the past year or year and a half, they have been talking about giving a new impetus to housing in the near future, and they are still talking about it. Since the unemployment rate is particularly alarming in Quebec, I think it is the duty of Quebec members to press the government to come up with suggestions, proposals and much more effective legislation than those put forward in the last years.

How can a new impetus be given to the housing industry in the short term? There has been a lack of realism, I think. The minister mentioned earlier that millions had been spent on housing. But we know very well that even those considerable amounts are not adequate considering the great number of people with a low income.
I am not in the habit of limiting myself to criticism. But I think that the pitiful failure of the government to provide housing for low-income groups should prompt us to press more strongly than ever for more effective measures on their behalf.
It was said that a number of housing units had been built, but the interest rate on mortgages, which can be most detrimental to the building industry, has always been glossed over.
I have already urged that loans at 5 or 6 per cent be made available to those earning $10,000 or less per year. I will be told: But who will pay the difference in interest? I will answer that it is obviously up to the government to make up the difference. However, I do not believe that easier loans, longer amortization periods up to 40 years will allow more Canadian citizens to purchase a house, for they will then have to pay for it three times over.
Reference is made to low-cost housing, and I think I am in a position to say a few words on this matter. This week, I got the happy news: in my constituency, more particularly in the city of Joliette, a $600,000 housing project will be built. Now those $600,000 can at the most allow the construction of 51 3 and 4 room dwellings and this is a 50-year loan bearing at 8 per cent interest. Therefore, the owners will have to pay a monthly rent of $136 for a 3-room dwelling and of $150 for a 4-room dwelling. I do not believe that this can be considered low-cost housing. Surely, this project is important for my area and this large city of my constituency. I appreciate the launching of the project, but I know very well that only professional people will benefit from it.
It is therefore our duty, as members of this House, to demand more realistic action for small wage-earners. We have the opportunity today to try again and ask the minister to be more compassionate and understanding and to make it possible for small wage-earners to live in adequate dwellings with suitable rents.
It is true that for several years, we have been asking the removal of that hateful 11 per cent tax on building materials. Reference
June 12, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES	8077
has been made to the possibility of granting loans to workers earning from $5,000 to $10,000 per year at an interest rate of 5 or 6 per cent. I venture to think that the government will react to those recommendations. We could be told that we are only criticizing. I think that our suggestions are acceptable. I am convinced that such a policy would likely give new life to the building industry in Quebec as elsewhere in Canada.
Indeed, the construction industry employs close to 30 per cent of the Canadian labour force. Somebody could say that there is the risk of inflation. Everything that is said about inflation makes me laugh, because the government policy to eliminate it made it worse. Inflation has never been so bad. Yet, the budgets of various departments were cut while more unemployment was created to eradicate inflation. The policy of the government in that regard did not produce the expected results.
Housing is not any better for all this. If the suggestions to get construction going again were implemented, thousands of new jobs would be created and industries would be more prosperous.
As for the 500,000 unemployed who receive from $53 to $60 a week, they could find work. They would pay small taxes on certain building materials. However, the general 11 per cent tax on building materials would have to be repealed.
Not wanting to deny my colleagues the opportunity of speaking-they probably have much to say-I conclude my remarks by saying that, like an important segment of the population, I am quite disappointed with the housing policy of this government. Of course, I have had the pleasure of approving the policy of the government in other fields, and I even made it a point to do so. As to the failure of the policy concerning housing and assistance to low wage earners, I feel it is my duty-and I do not think I am wrong in saying so-to hold the government responsible for it.
They can say all they want about establishing a department of urban affairs, about dialogue or co-operation between municipal, provincial and federal governments, but as long as we fail to reduce substantially the interest rate and to bring in legislation to lower the price of building materials, it will be completely ridiculous to talk about boosting the construction industry and the minister's wishes today will remain pious ones.
Request for Housing Statement
I dare hope that these few comments will incite the government to be more serious, more courageous and more sincere as regards the great number of people who need suitable housing at reasonable prices. It is the only way to offer them decent homes. That is the only way to put the building industry back on its feet. To speak at greater length on that subject would probably be a waste of time. I hope that the government will avail itself of these suggestions and that I will not be regarded as confining himself to destructive criticisms. On the contrary, while trying to make suggestions I keep hoping that the government will stop turning a deaf ear to the possibility of housing low income people in proper homes at reasonable prices.
Mr. Speaker, I think this would be a good show of humanitarianism, because we would then recognize that a homeowner is a precious asset for society, since the one who owns a home is always more interested in society than the tenant. The owners are more fully aware of their responsibilities, because they wish to protect their property. I suggest that to be able to afford an adequate home is an honor and something to be proud of. It would be within everybody's reach if reasonable interest rates were available and if materials were moderately priced. I do not see any other solution. I am not well versed in economics, but I think I can say that the economists who have come up with housing proposals so far have been way off the mark.
